questions.enonce_markdown:
A function $f : \mathbb{R} - \{-1\} \longrightarrow \mathbb{R} - \{1\}$ is defined by
$$f(x) = \frac{x - 1}{x + 1}.$$
Show that $f$ is surjective. (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
A function is surjective if every element of the codomain has at least one pre-image in the domain: for every $y \in \mathbb{R} - \{1\}$ there is some $x \in \mathbb{R} - \{-1\}$ with $f(x) = y$.

Let $y \in \mathbb{R} - \{1\}$ and solve $y = \dfrac{x - 1}{x + 1}$ for $x$:
$$y(x + 1) = x - 1 \;\Rightarrow\; yx + y = x - 1 \;\Rightarrow\; x(y - 1) = -1 - y \;\Rightarrow\; x = \frac{1 + y}{1 - y}.$$
This is defined because $y \ne 1$, so $x \in \mathbb{R}$.

It lies in the domain: $x = -1$ would need $1 + y = -(1 - y) = y - 1$, i.e. $1 = -1$, impossible. So $x \ne -1$.

Check: $f\!\left(\dfrac{1 + y}{1 - y}\right) = \dfrac{\frac{1 + y}{1 - y} - 1}{\frac{1 + y}{1 - y} + 1} = \dfrac{2y}{2} = y$.

Hence every $y \in \mathbb{R} - \{1\}$ is the image of $x = \dfrac{1 + y}{1 - y} \in \mathbb{R} - \{-1\}$, so $f$ is surjective. (The map is also well defined into $\mathbb{R} - \{1\}$: $\frac{x-1}{x+1} = 1$ would give $-1 = 1$.)
$$\boxed{f \text{ is surjective}}$$

questions.enonce_markdown: A function $f : \mathbb{R} - \{-1\} \longrightarrow \mathbb{R} - \{1\}$ is defined by $f(x) = \dfrac{x - 1}{x + 1}$. Find the composite function $(f \circ f)(x)$, stating its domain. (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
$$(f \circ f)(x) = f\big(f(x)\big) = \frac{f(x) - 1}{f(x) + 1}, \qquad f(x) = \frac{x - 1}{x + 1}.$$
Numerator and denominator over the common denominator $x + 1$:
$$f(x) - 1 = \frac{(x - 1) - (x + 1)}{x + 1} = \frac{-2}{x + 1}, \qquad f(x) + 1 = \frac{(x - 1) + (x + 1)}{x + 1} = \frac{2x}{x + 1}.$$
Therefore
$$(f \circ f)(x) = \frac{-2/(x + 1)}{2x/(x + 1)} = -\frac{1}{x}.$$

**Domain.** $x$ must be in the domain of $f$, so $x \ne -1$; and $f(x)$ must be in the domain of $f$, so $f(x) \ne -1$:
$$\frac{x - 1}{x + 1} = -1 \iff x - 1 = -x - 1 \iff x = 0.$$
So $x = 0$ must also be excluded. (The simplified expression $-\frac1x$ is undefined at $0$ for the same reason; at $x = -1$ the simplified rule would give $1$, but $-1$ is not in the domain of $f$, so it is excluded.)
$$\boxed{(f \circ f)(x) = -\frac1x, \quad \text{domain } \mathbb{R} - \{-1, 0\}}$$

questions.enonce_markdown: A function $f : \mathbb{R} - \{-1\} \longrightarrow \mathbb{R} - \{1\}$ is defined by $f(x) = \dfrac{x - 1}{x + 1}$. Determine whether $f \circ f(x)$ is an even or odd function. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
From part (b), $(f \circ f)(x) = -\dfrac1x$. Let $g(x) = (f \circ f)(x)$. Then
$$g(-x) = -\frac{1}{-x} = \frac1x = -\left(-\frac1x\right) = -g(x).$$
An even function satisfies $g(-x) = g(x)$ and an odd function satisfies $g(-x) = -g(x)$. Here $g(-x) = -g(x)$ for every $x$ for which both $x$ and $-x$ are admissible, and $g(-x) \ne g(x)$ (e.g. $g(2) = -\frac12$, $g(-2) = \frac12$). So $f \circ f$ is **odd** (its graph, the hyperbola $y = -\frac1x$, is symmetric about the origin).

Remark on the domain: strictly, the domain $\mathbb{R} - \{-1, 0\}$ of $f \circ f$ is not symmetric about $0$ (it contains $1$ but not $-1$), so on exactly that domain the parity condition cannot be checked at $x = 1$. The expected answer is that the rule $-\frac1x$ is an odd function.
$$\boxed{f \circ f \text{ is odd}}$$

questions.enonce_markdown: Expand $\dfrac{1 - x}{(1 + 2x)^{\frac13}}$ as a series in ascending powers of $x$ as far as the term in $x^2$. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Write the expression as $(1 - x)(1 + 2x)^{-1/3}$ and expand the binomial with $(1 + u)^n = 1 + nu + \dfrac{n(n - 1)}{2!}u^2 + \cdots$, $n = -\frac13$, $u = 2x$:
$$(1 + 2x)^{-1/3} = 1 + \left(-\frac13\right)(2x) + \frac{\left(-\frac13\right)\left(-\frac43\right)}{2}(2x)^2 + \cdots = 1 - \frac{2x}{3} + \frac29\cdot 4x^2 + \cdots = 1 - \frac{2}{3}x + \frac{8}{9}x^2 + \cdots$$
Multiply by $(1 - x)$ and keep terms up to $x^2$:
$$(1 - x)\left(1 - \frac23 x + \frac89 x^2\right) = 1 - \frac23 x + \frac89 x^2 - x + \frac23 x^2 + \cdots = 1 - \frac53 x + \frac{14}{9}x^2 + \cdots$$
The expansion is valid for $|2x| < 1$, i.e. $|x| < \frac12$.
$$\boxed{\frac{1 - x}{(1 + 2x)^{1/3}} = 1 - \frac53 x + \frac{14}{9}x^2 + \cdots}$$
